title: Power and energy transfer rate

learning_outcomes.text: define power as work done per unit time
solve problems using P = W / t

external_knowledge: 9702_t05_m01_o01: understand the concept of work, and recall and use work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force
Convert minutes and hours to seconds.
Use joules, seconds and watts consistently in calculations.
prerequisites.handoff_status: No controlled 9702_t05 lesson map, previous-lesson package or module summary exists in the repository. Only the official prior work outcome and basic unit skills are assumed.

prior_knowledge_summary: Work is an energy transfer caused by a force acting through a displacement.
For a constant force parallel to displacement, use W = Fs.
Energy and work are measured in joules, J, and time is measured in seconds, s.
new_learning: Power describes the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
Use P = ΔE/t to calculate average power over a time interval.
Rearrange the power relationship to find energy transferred or elapsed time.
Distinguish a transfer rate from the total energy transferred.
not_yet_taught: derivation and use of P = Fv
new gravitational potential energy or kinetic energy methods
electrical power formulae such as P = VI
efficiency calculations as new lesson content
instantaneous power for a continuously changing transfer rate

blocks.heading: Same energy, different race
content: Two pumps each move 2400 J of energy into water. Pump A takes 20 s. Pump B takes 80 s. The total energy transfer is equal, but the pumps are not equally powerful.
What quantity can distinguish a fast energy transfer from a slow one?

figure.purpose: Create the need for a rate quantity by comparing equal energy transfers over unequal times.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show two simple water pumps, each linked to a 2400 J energy card. Add separate clocks marked 20 s and 80 s. Leave which pump is more powerful as an unanswered prediction.
figure.alt_text: Two pumps transfer 2400 joules in different times.

blocks.heading: Power measures how quickly energy moves
content: Controlled definition: power is work done or energy transferred per unit time.
Formula to remember: P = ΔE/t.
P is power in watts, W. ΔE is energy transferred in joules, J. t is the time interval in seconds, s.
One watt means one joule transferred each second, so 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹. When work done W is the energy transfer, the same idea may be written P = W/t.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: work done or energy transferred per unit time

figure.purpose: Connect the verbal definition, formula and watt unit without treating power as an energy store.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show equal energy packets crossing a boundary during each one-second interval. Add the exact formula P = ΔE/t and unit statement 1 W = 1 J/s with sparse labels.
figure.alt_text: Energy packets transferred each second explain power and the watt.

blocks.heading: Compare the two pumps
content: For pump A, P = ΔE/t = 2400/20 = 120 W.
For pump B, P = 2400/80 = 30 W.
Pump A transfers the same energy in one quarter of the time, so its power is four times as large.
Independent check: 120 J transferred each second for 20 s gives 2400 J, and 30 J transferred each second for 80 s also gives 2400 J.

figure.purpose: Show that equal energy can correspond to different power and check each result by rebuilding the energy total.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use two aligned worked columns for 2400 J over 20 s and 2400 J over 80 s. Show 120 J and 30 J packets per one-second strip, then a separate multiplication check returning 2400 J in each column.
figure.alt_text: Two worked columns compare powers of 120 watts and 30 watts for equal energy transfers.

blocks.heading: Power is a rate, not an amount
content: Think of energy transfer like water passing through a pipe. Energy is the total amount that crosses. Power tells us how quickly it crosses.
A 600 W machine transfers 600 J each second while it runs. In 5.0 s it transfers ΔE = Pt = 600 × 5.0 = 3000 J.
A 150 W machine running for 40 s transfers 6000 J. The lower-power machine transfers more total energy because it runs much longer.

figure.purpose: Separate transfer rate from total transferred energy using a flow analogy and a numerical comparison.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. On the left, compare a wide short flow with a narrow long flow. On the right, show 600 W for 5.0 s gives 3000 J while 150 W for 40 s gives 6000 J. Label rate and total separately.
figure.alt_text: A fast short transfer and a slower long transfer separate power from total energy.

blocks.heading: Choose what the question asks for
content: If power and time are known, rearrange P = ΔE/t to ΔE = Pt. A 75 W mixer running for 2.0 min has t = 120 s, so ΔE = 75 × 120 = 9000 J.
If energy and power are known, rearrange to t = ΔE/P. A motor transferring 54 kJ at 300 W takes t = 54000/300 = 180 s.
Check the first answer through units: W × s = (J s⁻¹) × s = J. Check the second: J/W = J/(J s⁻¹) = s.

figure.purpose: Teach both rearrangements with unit checks and an explicit minute-to-second conversion.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a branching formula-choice layout: known P and t leads to ΔE = Pt; known ΔE and P leads to t = ΔE/P. Include the 75 W mixer and 300 W motor calculations with units on every line.
figure.alt_text: A formula-choice sketch shows how to calculate energy or time from power.

blocks.heading: Why the biggest energy number is not always the biggest power
content: It feels natural to compare only the energy values because a larger energy transfer sounds more powerful.
That comparison fails when the time intervals differ. A transfer of 12 kJ in 60 s has power 200 W, while 8.0 kJ in 20 s has power 400 W.
Always compare energy per second. Convert both energy and time to SI units before dividing.

figure.purpose: Repair the misconception that greater transferred energy necessarily means greater power.
figure.brief: Landscape 3:2 white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Compare 12 kJ over 60 s with 8.0 kJ over 20 s. Cross out the energy-only ranking, then highlight the correct 200 W and 400 W rate comparison.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows that the smaller energy transfer can have the greater power.

blocks.heading: A reliable power routine
content: First identify the energy transferred or work done over one stated interval. Next convert the interval to seconds. Then use P = ΔE/t and attach the watt unit.
If the question asks for energy or time, rearrange before substituting. Keep unrounded values until the final answer and check that the unit matches the requested quantity.
For a changing machine, this lesson calculates average power over the whole stated interval. It does not claim the rate was constant at every instant.

evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: All complete P2 records mapped to the two lesson outcomes were read. Only definition, energy-time calculation, comparison and multi-step rate demands are transferred into this lesson. Other-topic and later P = Fv demands remain excluded.

concepts_taught: power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy
average power over a stated time interval
the difference between transfer rate and total energy
misconceptions_addressed: Power and energy are the same physical quantity.
The process transferring more total energy must have greater power.
Minutes or kilojoules may be substituted without conversion when watts are required.
Average power proves that the transfer rate was constant at every instant.
next_lesson_can_assume: State the controlled definition of power.
Use and rearrange P = ΔE/t with SI units.
Compare energy-transfer rates over different intervals.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Derive or use P = Fv unless it is taught next.
Use new gravitational or kinetic energy methods not supplied by the question.
Treat average power as instantaneous power.
